To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mutations in the H2–H3 subdomain of the prion protein affect protein stability and conversion efficiency.
the designed mutations V175 and T187 in the H2 subdomain of the prion protein increase protein stability, but do not affect its conversion propensity.

the hydrophobic mutation V175I increases protein stability and in vitro fibrillisation propensity of PrP, while the mutation T187I increases protein stability, fibrillisation propensity, and conversion efficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of hydrophobic interactions on the stability and conversion of the prion protein.
the role of hydrophobicity of the H2-H2 subdomain in the conversion of PrP.
the role of subdomains in PrP conversion and the effect of hydrophobic interactions on PrP stability and fibrilization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hydrophobicity of the H2-H4 subdomain is not the key feature for prion protein conversion.
increasing hydrophobic interactions in the H2 subdomain does not necessarily increase conversion efficiency.
the effect of mutations on PrP stability and fibrillization is complex and depends on their position and the type of mutation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydrophobicity of the subdomain H2-H3 is not a crucial factor for prion conversion.
hydrophobic mutations in H2-H3 domain increase protein stability, fibrillization propensity and conversion efficiency.
increasing hydrophobicity in H2-H3 domain of PrP leads to increased stability and conversion efficiency of prion protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increasing the hydrophobity of the H2-H2 subdomain of PrP does not necessarily increase the fibrillization propensity, but may increase the conversion efficiency.
increasing hydrophobic interactions in the H2 subdomain can be beneficial in prion protein conversion, and the designed T187I mutation is the most efficient in this regard.
hydrophobic interactions are important for PrP fibrillization, however the nature of the hydrophobic residues is also critical for conversion.
